new_quiz.q: What is UE_LOG?
choices: The C++ macro that writes a message to the Output Log
The file where the editor saves its settings
The window that shows compile errors
The console command that clears the screen
new_quiz.explain: UE_LOG is how C++ code writes a line to the Output Log. Each call names a category, a verbosity and a text.

new_quiz.q: What is a log category?
choices: The color of a message
The time at which a message was written
A name shown in front of the message, which messages belong to
The folder where log files are stored
new_quiz.explain: Every message belongs to a category, and its name appears in front of the text. LogUU in front of a line tells you the message is yours.

new_quiz.q: What does the verbosity of a log message say?
choices: How long the message is
How serious the message is
Which actor wrote the message
How often the message repeats
new_quiz.explain: Verbosity is the level of a message. Log is normal information, Warning points at a possible problem, and Error reports a real one.

new_quiz.q: Which macro declares the category LogUU in a header file?
choices: DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY
UE_LOG
UPROPERTY
DECLARE_LOG_CATEGORY_EXTERN
new_quiz.explain: DECLARE_LOG_CATEGORY_EXTERN in a header tells other files that the category exists. Every file that includes the header can then log to it.

new_quiz.q: Which macro defines the category in a .cpp file?
choices: DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY
DECLARE_LOG_CATEGORY_EXTERN
UFUNCTION
TRACE_CPUPROFILER_EVENT_SCOPE
new_quiz.explain: The category is declared in the header and defined once in a .cpp file with DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY. Both parts are needed.

new_quiz.q: Why do you create your own log category?
choices: So your messages are written faster
So your messages are hidden from other people
So you can filter the log to see only your messages
So your messages are saved in the project folder
new_quiz.explain: The engine writes a lot of text to the Output Log. With your own category, one filter shows only the lines from your code.

new_quiz.q: With which three verbosity levels do you write messages in this quest?
choices: Low, Medium and High
Log, Warning and Error
Debug, Release and Shipping
Start, Update and End
new_quiz.explain: You write one message each with Log, Warning and Error. In the Output Log you can then see how the levels differ.

new_quiz.q: Which of the three verbosity levels you use is the most serious?
choices: Log
Warning
They are all equal
Error
new_quiz.explain: Error is the most serious of the three, Warning is in the middle, and Log is plain information.

new_quiz.q: How do you see only your own messages in the Output Log?
choices: Set the filter so that it shows only the LogUU category
Close and open the Output Log again
Rename the actor to LogUU
Press F9 in the Output Log
new_quiz.explain: The filter of the Output Log can show single categories. With only LogUU selected, every other line is hidden.

new_quiz.q: With the log command in the console you set LogUU to the verbosity Warning. Which of your three messages no longer appears?
choices: The one with the verbosity Error
The one with the verbosity Log
The one with the verbosity Warning
All three still appear
new_quiz.explain: The command sets the lowest level that the category still shows. With Warning, messages of the lower level Log are dropped, while Warning and Error still appear.

new_quiz.q: Which pattern do most Unreal projects use to combine C++ and Blueprint?
choices: All logic in the Level Blueprint and all data in C++
One C++ class for each Blueprint node
A C++ base class with the core logic, and a Blueprint child where designers set values
Blueprints for the editor and C++ for the packaged game
new_quiz.explain: The base class in C++ holds the logic that should not break. The Blueprint child is where designers set values and add small changes.

new_quiz.q: What does the way you split the work between C++ and Blueprint decide?
choices: Who can change what without asking a programmer
How many levels the game can have
Which engine version the project uses
How large the textures may be
new_quiz.explain: Everything exposed to Blueprint can be changed by designers themselves. Everything kept in C++ needs a programmer.

new_quiz.q: Which kind of work does the Epic page name as a strength of Blueprint?
choices: Tight loops over large sets of data
Low-level access to external libraries
Merging changes from many programmers
Scripting behaviors and prototyping with fast iteration
new_quiz.explain: Blueprint is quick to change and easy to read as a visual flow. That makes it good for defining behavior and for trying ideas.

new_quiz.q: Which kind of work does the Epic page name as better done in C++?
choices: Setting the color of a single prop
Core systems and code where performance matters, such as tight loops
Trying out a new idea in ten minutes
Choosing which mesh a pickup shows
new_quiz.explain: C++ is the foundation for systems. The cost of Blueprint shows most in core code, tight loops, large data sets and many ticking instances.

new_quiz.q: Why does C++ code run faster than Blueprint logic?
choices: C++ compiles to machine code, while Blueprint runs in a virtual machine
C++ code is shorter than a Blueprint graph
Blueprint only runs on every second frame
C++ skips the collision checks
new_quiz.explain: Machine code runs directly on the processor. Blueprint bytecode is run by a virtual machine, which adds a small cost to every node.

new_quiz.q: Why is C++ easier to work on in a team with version control?
choices: C++ files cannot be edited by two people
C++ files are saved more often
C++ is text, so changes are easy to compare and merge
C++ files are smaller than textures
new_quiz.explain: Text files can be compared line by line and merged. A Blueprint is a binary asset, where two edits cannot be combined that way.

new_quiz.q: What is a specifier in the UPROPERTY macro?
choices: A comment for other programmers
The type of the variable
The default value of the variable
A word that controls what the editor and Blueprints can do
new_quiz.explain: Specifiers such as EditDefaultsOnly or BlueprintReadOnly set the access to a value. Choosing them is how you decide what designers may touch.

new_quiz.q: What does the specifier EditDefaultsOnly allow?
choices: The value can be edited on every placed copy in the level
The value can be edited in the class defaults, but not on placed copies
The value can be edited only in C++
The value can be edited only while the game runs
new_quiz.explain: EditDefaultsOnly shows the value in the class defaults. A designer sets it once per Blueprint child, and single copies in the level cannot differ.

new_quiz.q: What does the specifier BlueprintReadOnly allow?
choices: Blueprint graphs can read the value but not change it
Blueprint graphs can change the value but not read it
Blueprint graphs cannot see the value
Blueprint graphs can delete the value
new_quiz.explain: BlueprintReadOnly gives graphs a get node only. The value stays under the control of the C++ code.

new_quiz.q: What is a delegate?
choices: A copy of a class in another module
A variable that stores a number
A signal that other code can listen to
A person who reviews your code
new_quiz.explain: A delegate announces that something happened. When Blueprints can assign to it, designers can react to that event without any change to the C++ code.

new_quiz.q: How do programmers and other team members often share the work on an actor?
choices: Programmers write a base class in C++, and other people build on it with Blueprint children
Programmers write Blueprints, and other people rewrite them in C++
Everyone edits the same Blueprint at the same time
Programmers place the actors, and other people compile them
new_quiz.explain: The C++ base class holds the logic. Blueprint children made from it let other people create variants without writing code.

new_quiz.q: Which three things must a good base class offer to the people who build on it?
choices: It must be short, private and final
It must be easy to tune, warn clearly when it is set up wrong, and be explained in writing
It must have many components, many functions and many files
It must run every frame, save itself and load itself
new_quiz.explain: Other people use your class without reading its code. They need values to tune, warnings that explain mistakes, and a text that says how it works.

new_quiz.q: Where do you build the components of the base actor?
choices: In BeginPlay
In the Tick function
In the README
In the constructor
new_quiz.explain: The constructor is the function that runs when the object is created. Components created there are part of the actor from the start, and every Blueprint child gets them.

new_quiz.q: How do you make values tunable for the people who use your class?
choices: You write them into the README
You type them into the function bodies
You expose them with UPROPERTY
You store them in the log category
new_quiz.explain: A variable marked with UPROPERTY and the right specifiers appears in the editor. A Blueprint child can then set it with no code change.

new_quiz.q: What does the BlueprintNativeEvent in your base class give to the Blueprint children?
choices: A function that they cannot change
A default version in C++ that a child may override
A function that only runs in the editor
A component that is added at BeginPlay
new_quiz.explain: The default behavior works without any Blueprint work. A child that needs something else overrides the event.

new_quiz.q: How do you declare and define your own log category, for example LogUU?
choices: With DECLARE_LOG_CATEGORY_EXTERN and DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY
With UCLASS and UPROPERTY
With CreateDefaultSubobject and SetupAttachment
With UE_LOG and UFUNCTION
new_quiz.explain: The first macro declares the category in a header and the second defines it in a .cpp file. Your messages then appear under your own category name.

new_quiz.q: For which cases do you add clear warnings to the actor?
choices: For every frame in which the actor ticks
For every time the actor is placed in a level
For every value that a designer changes
For the cases where the actor is set up badly
new_quiz.explain: A designer may forget a mesh or leave a reference empty. A clear warning in the log tells them what is wrong, so they can fix it without you.

new_quiz.q: In what may the 2 Blueprint children differ?
choices: In their C++ parent class
In their whole logic
Only in their data and in one override
Only in their names
new_quiz.explain: If two variants need nothing more than other values and one override, the base class does its job. All shared logic stays in C++.

new_quiz.q: What must your README say?
choices: How long you worked on the class and which IDE you used
What is in C++, what is in Blueprint, and how a designer would add a third child
Which engine source files you read
Every line of the header file, copied as text
new_quiz.explain: The README is the manual for the next person. With it, a designer can make a third child without asking you.

new_quiz.q: What does the short video clip have to show?
choices: Both Blueprint children working in Play in Editor
The build output of the IDE
The README opened in a text editor
The constructor running in the debugger
new_quiz.explain: The clip proves that the base class works through its children. Both children must be seen working in the test level.

new_quiz.q: Through which part does the Character class in Unreal move?
choices: The Static Mesh component
The Sky Light
The Character Movement component
The Output Log
new_quiz.explain: The Character Movement component does the moving for a Character. It has values such as walk speed and jump height.

new_quiz.q: Why do movement values such as walk speed and jump height matter so much?
choices: They decide how the game feels to play
They decide how large the level is
They decide which engine version is needed
They decide how many players can join
new_quiz.explain: A small change in speed or jump height changes the feel of every moment of play. This is why they must be easy to tune.

new_quiz.q: What is the gain of setting movement values up in C++ and exposing them?
choices: The values can never be changed again
The character moves without any input
The values are hidden from the editor
A Blueprint child can tune them without changing any code
new_quiz.explain: The logic stays in C++. Designers open the Blueprint child and change the numbers there.

new_quiz.q: From which class does the character class of the tutorial page, AAdventureCharacter, inherit?
choices: AActor
ACharacter
UActorComponent
UDataAsset
new_quiz.explain: ACharacter already has a Character Movement component and functions such as Jump. Your class builds on it.

new_quiz.q: Which inherited function applies movement in a direction when the player uses the move input?
choices: CreateDefaultSubobject
SetupAttachment
AddMovementInput
DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY
new_quiz.explain: AddMovementInput tells the character to move along a direction. The Character Movement component then turns this into real movement.

new_quiz.q: How is the jump connected to the input on the tutorial page?
choices: The Started event calls Jump, and the Completed event calls StopJumping
The Completed event calls Jump, and the Started event calls StopJumping
Both events call AddMovementInput
The jump is called on every Tick
new_quiz.explain: Pressing the key starts the jump and releasing it stops the jump. Jump and StopJumping are functions that the Character class already has.

new_quiz.q: In which function are the input actions bound to your movement functions?
choices: In the constructor
In Tick
In the README
In SetupPlayerInputComponent
new_quiz.explain: SetupPlayerInputComponent is where the character connects input to code. BindAction links each Input Action to one of your functions.

new_quiz.q: What does the Blueprint child of the character assign on the tutorial page?
choices: The C++ source files of the class
The input assets, such as the mapping context and the move and jump actions
The log category of the project
The build configuration
new_quiz.explain: The C++ class has properties for the input assets. In the Blueprint child you pick the real assets, so code and content stay apart.

new_quiz.q: How do you expose a movement value so that a Blueprint child can tune it?
choices: Write the value into a comment
Make the variable private with no macro
Mark a variable with UPROPERTY and a specifier such as EditAnywhere
Print the value with UE_LOG
new_quiz.explain: UPROPERTY makes the variable known to the editor, and the specifier allows editing. The value then appears in the Details panel of the Blueprint child.

new_quiz.q: What does your screenshot have to show?
choices: The tuned values in a Blueprint child
The build output of the IDE
The character in a packaged game
The tutorial page in a browser
new_quiz.explain: The two values you exposed must be visible and changed in a Blueprint child. That proves a designer could tune them without code.

new_quiz.q: What is a Data Asset?
choices: A node that reads a file from disk
A file in the Content Browser that stores a set of values
A mesh with data painted on its vertices
A log category for item messages
new_quiz.explain: A Data Asset only holds values, such as the name and price of an item. It has no logic of its own.

new_quiz.q: What do designers gain when a programmer defines the Data Asset class in C++?
choices: They can change the C++ code in the editor
They no longer need the Content Browser
They get one item that cannot be changed
They can create as many item files as they need without touching code
new_quiz.explain: The class defines which fields an item has. Each new item is then only a new asset that a designer fills in.

new_quiz.q: From which class does the item class of the tutorial page, UItemDefinition, inherit?
choices: UDataAsset
AActor
ACharacter
UActorComponent
new_quiz.explain: A class that inherits from UDataAsset can be chosen when you create a Data Asset in the editor.

new_quiz.q: How do you create an item asset from your class in the editor?
choices: Drag the header file into the level
Click Add, then User Interface, then Widget Blueprint
In the Content Browser, open Miscellaneous, choose Data Asset and select your class
Open Tools, then New C++ Class
new_quiz.explain: Data Asset is in the Miscellaneous group of the Content Browser menu. A window then asks which class the new asset should use.

new_quiz.q: What does the idea of data-driven gameplay on the tutorial page mean?
choices: The game downloads its data from a server
Values are kept as data in a central place and are not hardcoded in the logic
The player types data during the game
Every value is written into the function bodies
new_quiz.explain: Data and logic are kept apart. Items can be added or changed in data, and the code that uses them stays the same.

new_quiz.q: On the tutorial page the struct FItemData inherits from FTableRowBase. What does this make possible?
choices: The struct can tick every frame
The struct can be placed in a level
The struct can be compiled without a header
The struct can be used as a row of a Data Table
new_quiz.explain: A Data Table is like a spreadsheet whose rows all have the same struct. That struct must be based on FTableRowBase.

new_quiz.q: The tutorial page defines the enum EItemType with UENUM(BlueprintType). What is this enum for?
choices: It gives each item a type from a fixed list
It stores the price of each item
It holds the mesh of each item
It counts how many items exist
new_quiz.explain: An enum is a fixed list of named choices. BlueprintType makes it usable in Blueprints and in the editor.

new_quiz.q: The item class holds its mesh as a TSoftObjectPtr. What is special about this kind of reference?
choices: It copies the mesh into the Data Asset
It can only point to textures
It points to an asset without loading it until it is needed
It deletes the mesh when the item is used
new_quiz.explain: A soft reference stores where the asset is. The mesh is only loaded when the game asks for it, so a list of many items stays light.

new_quiz.q: You created an item asset, but the fields of your class do not show in the editor. What do you check first in the C++ class?
choices: That the class has a Tick function
That each field is marked with UPROPERTY and a specifier such as EditAnywhere
That the class name starts with A
That the class has a log category
new_quiz.explain: The editor only shows fields that reflection knows. UPROPERTY with EditAnywhere makes a field visible and editable in the asset.

new_quiz.q: What does your screenshot have to show?
choices: The header file in the IDE
A pickup in a packaged game
The tutorial page in a browser
2 Data Assets made from your C++ class
new_quiz.explain: Two item assets from one class prove the point of the quest: the class is written once, and items are made as data.

new_quiz.q: Why should you measure code before you try to make it faster?
choices: Measuring makes the code faster by itself
The compiler refuses to build code that was not measured
The slow part is often not where you expect
Measuring removes the need for testing
new_quiz.explain: Guessing often leads you to change code that was never the problem. A measurement shows where the time really goes.

new_quiz.q: What is Unreal Insights?
choices: The tool that records where the engine spends its time
The window that lists compile errors
The page that documents the C++ classes
The plugin that writes log files
new_quiz.explain: Unreal Insights is the profiling tool of the engine. It shows the work of each frame on a timeline.

new_quiz.q: What is a trace?
choices: A line that connects two nodes
A recording that Unreal Insights can open
A breakpoint in the IDE
A warning in the Output Log
new_quiz.explain: A trace is the recording of what the engine did over a period of time. You capture it while the game runs and study it afterwards.

new_quiz.q: What is a named CPU scope?
choices: A limit on how much CPU time the game may use
A list of all functions of a class
A setting that makes code run on another thread
A mark around your own code that gives it its own name in the trace
new_quiz.explain: The scope measures the time spent in the marked code. In the trace, that time is shown as a block with the name you gave it.

new_quiz.q: Which macro adds a named CPU scope?
choices: TRACE_CPUPROFILER_EVENT_SCOPE
DECLARE_LOG_CATEGORY_EXTERN
UE_LOG
UFUNCTION
new_quiz.explain: TRACE_CPUPROFILER_EVENT_SCOPE marks the code that follows it inside the function. The time until the function ends is recorded under the given name.

new_quiz.q: Why is a Tick function with some work in it a good place for your first scope?
choices: Tick runs only once, so the trace stays small
Tick cannot be measured in another way
Tick runs every frame, so the scope appears in the trace again and again
Tick is the only function that may contain macros
new_quiz.explain: A function that runs every frame is easy to find in a trace of 10 seconds. The work inside gives the scope a visible length.

new_quiz.q: How do you capture a trace from the editor?
choices: Open Window, then Output Log, and type trace
Click Trace at the bottom of the editor, choose Start Trace, play, then Stop Trace
Press F9 on the actor in the level
Build the project with the configuration Development Editor
new_quiz.explain: Start Trace begins the recording and Stop Trace ends it. In between, you play for about 10 seconds so that the trace has frames to show.

new_quiz.q: Where in Unreal Insights do you find your scope?
choices: In the Content Browser
In the Details panel
In the World Settings
In the timing view
new_quiz.explain: The timing view shows each frame as blocks of work on the threads. Your scope is one of these blocks, with the name you gave it.

new_quiz.q: You open the trace, but your named scope is nowhere to be found. What do you check first?
choices: That the actor was placed in the level, so its function ran during the trace
That the scope name is written in capital letters
That the level has a Directional Light
That the Output Log was open during play
new_quiz.explain: A scope is only recorded when its code runs. If the actor is not in the level, its function is never called and nothing is recorded.

new_quiz.q: Why should you give your scopes clear names?
choices: Short names make the code run faster
Unnamed scopes stop the build
So that you and other people can find them in a trace
So that the scope is saved in the Blueprint
new_quiz.explain: A trace has thousands of blocks. A clear name is what lets someone search for your code and understand what the block measures.
